name: ATTINY84A-SSUR
title: ATtiny24A/44A/84A 8-bit AVR microcontrollers with 2/4/8 Kbytes in-system programmable Flash
summary: A family of three low-power 8-bit AVR RISC microcontrollers that run most of their 120 instructions in one clock, at up to 20 MHz from 4.5 V to 5.5 V and down to 1.8 V at 4 MHz. They differ only in memory: 2, 4 or 8 Kbytes of self-programmable Flash with 128, 256 or 512 bytes each of EEPROM and SRAM. Around the core sit an 8-bit and a 16-bit timer with two PWM outputs each, a 10-bit ADC with eight single-ended inputs and twelve differential pairs with 1x or 20x gain, an analog comparator, the USI serial interface, a watchdog with its own oscillator, a calibrated 8 MHz RC oscillator, a temperature sensor and twelve I/O lines, all with pin-change interrupts. ATTINY84A-SSUR is the 8 Kbyte device in the 14-pin SOIC for -40 °C to 85 °C.
key_figures: 8-bit AVR RISC, 32 x 8 working registers, approaching 1 MIPS per MHz
8 Kbytes Flash, 512 bytes EEPROM, 512 bytes SRAM
10-bit, 8 single-ended channels, 12 differential pairs with 1x/20x gain
12 programmable I/O lines, pin-change interrupt on all 12

circuits.title: External clock drive configuration
circuits.description: An outside clock source feeds CLKI (PB0) and shares the part's ground. The CKSEL fuses must read 0000 for this source to clock the part; PB1 stays free for I/O.
notes: A cycle-to-cycle frequency step above 2% is not allowed; hold the part in reset across larger changes.

circuits.title: Crystal oscillator connections
circuits.description: A quartz crystal or ceramic resonator sits between XTAL1 (PB0) and XTAL2 (PB1), with a load capacitor from each pin to ground. C1 and C2 are equal; 12 pF to 22 pF suits crystals from 0.9 MHz up, while a ceramic resonator takes the values its own maker gives. The same hook-up serves a 32.768 kHz watch crystal on the low-frequency oscillator, whose internal load is 16 pF on XTAL1 and 6 pF on XTAL2.

circuits.title: debugWIRE connection
circuits.description: The part powered from 1.8 V to 5.5 V with its RESET pin (PB3) wired to the debugger's dW line, the single bidirectional wire that carries debug traffic once the DWEN fuse is programmed and the lock bits are clear.
notes: A pull-up on dW/RESET is optional; if fitted it must be 10 kΩ to 20 kΩ.
RESET tied straight to VCC stops debugWIRE working; capacitors on RESET and all external reset sources must be disconnected.

circuits.title: Serial programming connection
circuits.description: In-system programming over SPI: the programmer drives MOSI (PA6) and SCK (PA4), reads MISO (PA5), and holds RESET (PB3) low for the whole session, with the part powered from 1.8 V to 5.5 V.
notes: Running from the internal oscillator, CLKI (PB0) needs no clock source.

circuits.title: High-voltage serial programming connection
circuits.description: High-voltage serial programming: 11.5 V to 12.5 V on PB3 (RESET) and 4.5 V to 5.5 V on VCC, with PA0 to PA2 grounded as the Prog_enable code. The programmer clocks SCI into PB0, sends data on SDI (PA6) and instructions on SII (PA5), and reads SDO from PA4.
notes: SCI period at least 220 ns.

operation.text: Low-power CMOS 8-bit parts on the AVR enhanced RISC core. One instruction per clock for most of the set gives close to 1 MIPS per MHz. All 32 working registers connect straight to the ALU, so one instruction can read two registers and finish in a single cycle.
Projected from qualification: retention failures stay far below 1 PPM for 20 years at 85°C, and for 100 years at 25°C.

Harvard design: program and data have their own memories and buses. A single-level pipeline fetches the next instruction while the current one executes, so an instruction can complete every clock. The register file holds 32 x 8-bit registers with single-cycle access; R26 to R31 pair up as the 16-bit X, Y and Z pointers for indirect data addressing, and Z also points into Flash for lookup tables. Most instructions are one 16-bit word; some are 32 bits. Jumps and calls reach the whole address space.

The ALU does arithmetic, logic and bit operations between two registers, or a register and a constant, in one clock. SREG reports the result of the last arithmetic instruction after every ALU operation. SREG is not saved on interrupt entry nor restored on return; software does that.

The stack lives in SRAM and grows downward. The program must set SP above 0x60 before any call or enabled interrupt; at reset SP holds RAMEND. PUSH lowers SP by one, a call or interrupt by two; POP raises it by one, RET and RETI by two. SP is two 8-bit I/O registers, SPH and SPL.
The CPU runs on clkCPU straight from the selected clock source with no internal division. An ALU operation on two registers fetches the operands, executes and writes back within one clock.

Reset and each interrupt have their own vector at the bottom of program memory; the lower the vector address, the higher the priority, RESET first and INT0 next. Each interrupt has its own enable bit, used together with the global I bit in SREG. Entering an interrupt clears I, and RETI sets it again; software may set I inside a handler to allow nesting. Flag-type interrupts set a flag that hardware clears on vectoring, or software clears by writing one; a flag raised while disabled waits until enabled. Level-type interrupts last only while the condition does and may have no flag. After a return, one instruction of the main program always runs before a pending interrupt is taken. CLI takes effect at once; the instruction after SEI runs before any pending interrupt.

At least four clocks pass before the vector runs, while the PC is pushed; the usual jump at the vector adds three. An interrupt arriving during a multi-cycle instruction waits for it to finish. Waking from sleep adds four clocks on top of the start-up time. A return from interrupt takes four clocks: the two-byte PC is popped, SP rises by two and I is set.

2K/4K/8K bytes organised as 1024/2048/4096 x 16, since every instruction is 16 or 32 bits wide, rated for at least 10,000 write/erase cycles. The PC is 10/11/12 bits wide. Constant tables may sit anywhere in program memory (LPM, SPM). The Flash can be loaded serially through the SPI pins.

Data space starts with the 32 registers, then 64 I/O registers, then 128/256/512 bytes of SRAM from 0x0060. Five addressing modes reach it: direct (the whole space), indirect with displacement (63 locations from Y or Z), plain indirect, and indirect with post-increment or pre-decrement. An SRAM access takes two clkCPU cycles.

128/256/512 bytes in their own data space, read and written a byte at a time, rated for at least 100,000 write/erase cycles. A read stalls the CPU for four clocks, a write for two. A write needs the EEMPE-then-EEPE sequence: EEPE must be written within four cycles of EEMPE. The EEPMn bits pick atomic erase-and-write (00), erase only (01) or write only (10); EEPE stays set until the operation ends, and no other EEPROM operation can start meanwhile. Splitting erase and write lets a time-critical write later take only the write time, on a byte erased beforehand; a write to a byte not erased first leaves its contents undefined. The calibrated RC oscillator times the EEPROM, so its frequency must stay within the range given for OSCCAL. EEAR resets undefined; EEAR8 exists only on ATtiny84A.

Too low a VCC can corrupt EEPROM data, both because the write needs a minimum voltage and because the CPU can misexecute. Holding the part in reset while the supply is too low avoids it: enable the internal BOD, or use an external low-VCC reset if the BOD levels do not suit. A write under way when reset arrives still completes if the supply is high enough.

64 I/O addresses hold the peripheral control registers; they are reached with IN/OUT at 0x00-0x3F or as data space at 0x20-0x5F (add 0x20 for LD/ST). Addresses 0x00-0x1F are bit-addressable with SBI, CBI, SBIS and SBIC; on those, SBI and CBI touch only the named bit, so they are safe on flags cleared by writing one. Reserved bits are written as zero and reserved addresses are never written. Three general purpose I/O registers can hold global variables and flags.

A clock multiplexer picks the source (external clock, calibrated 8 MHz RC, 128 kHz RC, low-frequency crystal or crystal/resonator oscillator) and the system clock prescaler divides it. Four domains come out: clkCPU for the core, registers and stack; clkI/O for most peripherals such as the timers and the external interrupt logic, though some external interrupts are sensed asynchronously and work with clkI/O stopped; clkFLASH for the Flash interface, normally running with clkCPU; and clkADC, a separate domain so the CPU and I/O clocks can stop during a conversion to cut digital noise. The watchdog and reset logic run from the separate watchdog oscillator.

On wake from power-down the selected source itself times the start-up so the oscillator is stable before code runs. From reset an extra delay, counted on the watchdog oscillator (512 cycles for 4 ms, 8K cycles for 64 ms), lets the supply settle. SUT and CKSEL fuses set both.

CKSEL = 0000 takes the clock on CLKI. The applied frequency must not change by more than 2% between cycles, or behaviour is unpredictable; hold the part in reset during such changes. The system clock prescaler changes the frequency safely at run time.

CKSEL = 0010 selects it, needing no external parts. It depends on voltage and temperature. At reset hardware loads the factory calibration byte into OSCCAL; writing OSCCAL from software can calibrate it more closely. The watchdog oscillator still clocks the watchdog and the reset time-out.
CKSEL = 0100 selects a low-power 128 kHz oscillator whose frequency varies with supply, temperature and batch.
CKSEL = 0110 runs a 32.768 kHz watch crystal on XTAL1/XTAL2, with built-in load capacitance of 16 pF on XTAL1 and 6 pF on XTAL2. The crystal's own datasheet gives suitable capacitors.

XTAL1 is the input and XTAL2 the output of an inverting amplifier that can run a quartz crystal or a ceramic resonator. C1 and C2 are always equal; the best value depends on the crystal, stray capacitance and the electrical noise around it. CKSEL[3:1] picks one of the frequency-range modes, and CKSEL0 with SUT[1:0] picks the start-up time.

Parts ship with CKSEL = 0010, SUT = 10 and CKDIV8 programmed: the 8 MHz RC oscillator divided by 8, a 1.0 MHz system clock, with the longest start-up. Below 2.7 V the part is rated for 4 MHz at most, so unprogramming CKDIV8 there runs it at 8 MHz, beyond its rating.

CLKPR divides the system clock, with any source, to save power; clkI/O, clkADC, clkCPU and clkFLASH all scale. Changing the setting makes no glitch and no intermediate frequency above either the old or the new one. The prescaler's ripple counter runs at the undivided clock, so its state cannot be known and the exact switch time cannot be predicted.

With the CKOUT fuse programmed the system clock, after the prescaler, comes out on CKOUT (PB2), overriding the pin's normal I/O, from any clock source including the RC oscillator. The clock is not output during reset.

Setting SE in MCUCR and executing SLEEP enters the mode picked by SM[1:0]: 00 Idle, 01 ADC Noise Reduction, 10 Power-down, 11 Standby. An enabled interrupt wakes the part; it halts four cycles plus the start-up time, runs the handler, then continues after SLEEP with registers and SRAM intact. A reset during sleep restarts from the reset vector. A level interrupt used to wake must be held long enough for the wake-up to finish. Set SE just before SLEEP and clear it on waking.

Stops clkCPU and clkFLASH; the analog comparator, ADC, timers, watchdog and interrupts keep running, and both external and internal interrupts such as a timer overflow wake the part. Turning the comparator off with ACD saves power when its interrupt is not needed. An enabled ADC starts a conversion on entry.

Stops clkI/O, clkCPU and clkFLASH; the ADC, external interrupts and watchdog keep running. An enabled ADC starts a conversion on entry. Wake sources: ADC conversion complete, external, watchdog or brown-out reset, SPM/EEPROM ready, an INT0 level interrupt and pin change.

Stops the oscillator and every generated clock; only asynchronous modules run. External interrupts and the watchdog keep working if enabled. Wake sources: external, watchdog or brown-out reset, an INT0 level interrupt and pin change.
With SM = 11 and a crystal or resonator clock selected: Power-down with the oscillator left running, so the part wakes in six clocks.

A BOD enabled by fuse keeps watching VCC in sleep; setting BODS turns it off in Power-down and Standby, bringing sleep current down to the level with the BOD fused off. BODS is written by a timed sequence: set BODS and BODSE together, then within four clocks set BODS with BODSE clear. BODS is active three clocks after it is set and clears itself automatically after three clocks, so SLEEP must run while it is active. The BOD switches off on entering sleep and back on at wake-up; wake-up from sleep then takes approximately 60 µs.

PRR stops the clock to single peripherals in Active and Idle mode. A stopped peripheral keeps its state frozen, its registers cannot be read or written, and the resources it holds stay taken. Disable the peripheral before stopping its clock; clearing the bit brings it back in its earlier state. In the other sleep modes these clocks are already off.

Use the deepest sleep mode the application allows and turn off what is not needed. An enabled ADC stays on in every sleep mode; after it is turned off and on, the next conversion is an extended one. Turn the analog comparator off in Idle (if unused) and in ADC Noise Reduction; in the other modes it switches off by itself. A comparator set to use the internal reference must be turned off in every sleep mode, or the reference stays on. A fuse-enabled BOD and an enabled watchdog draw current in every sleep mode, a large share in the deep ones. The internal reference is on whenever the BOD, comparator or ADC needs it and needs its start-up time when turned back on. Port pins should not drive resistive loads. With both clkI/O and clkADC stopped the digital input buffers are off except where needed for wake-up. A floating input or one near VCC/2 draws heavy current through an enabled input buffer; on analog inputs keep the digital buffer off with DIDR0 at all times.

On reset every I/O register returns to its initial value and execution starts at the reset vector, which should hold an RJMP to the reset routine; a program that enables no interrupt can use the vector area for code. The I/O ports go to their reset state at once, with no clock needed. Once every reset source is released, a delay counter set by the SUT and CKSEL fuses stretches the internal reset so the supply can settle.

Four sources: power-on reset while VCC is under VPOT; external reset while RESET is held low past the minimum pulse width (when RESET is enabled); watchdog reset when the watchdog period runs out with the watchdog enabled; and brown-out reset while VCC is under VBOT with the BOD enabled. MCUSR flags which one occurred (PORF, EXTRF, BORF, WDRF).

An on-chip detector holds reset while VCC is below its threshold. Crossing it upward starts the time-out tTOUT; falling below it asserts reset again without delay. RESET may be tied to VCC, or held low externally to extend the start-up.

A low level on an enabled RESET pin longer than the minimum pulse width resets the part, even with no clock running; shorter pulses may not. When the pin rises past VRST the time-out tTOUT starts the part.

The on-chip BOD compares VCC with a trigger level chosen by the BODLEVEL fuses, with hysteresis. Falling below VBOT- asserts reset at once; rising above VBOT+ starts the time-out tTOUT. A dip shorter than tBOD is not detected.
On time-out the watchdog issues a one-CK reset pulse; its falling edge starts the time-out tTOUT.

A bandgap reference, varying with supply and temperature, serves the BOD and can feed the analog comparator or the ADC. It is on only when the BOD is fuse-enabled, when ACBG connects it to the comparator, or when the ADC is enabled. If the BOD is off, allow its start-up time after setting ACBG or enabling the ADC before using the result. Avoiding all three conditions turns it off for lowest power-down current.

Runs from its own 128 kHz on-chip oscillator through a prescaler with ten selectable periods (2K to 1024K oscillator cycles). WDR restarts it, as do disabling it and a chip reset. On time-out it resets the part, or it can raise an interrupt instead, useful for waking from Power-down. The WDTON fuse picks the safety level. Level 1 (WDTON unprogrammed): off at start, enabled freely by writing WDE; turning it off needs the timed sequence. Level 2 (WDTON programmed): always on and WDE reads one; changing the period needs the timed sequence. The sequence: write WDCE and WDE as one together, then within four clocks write the new WDE and WDP bits with WDCE clear.

INT0 and the twelve PCINT pins trigger interrupts even when set as outputs, which allows software interrupts. PCI0 fires when any enabled PCINT[7:0] pin toggles, PCI1 for PCINT[11:8]; PCMSK0 and PCMSK1 choose the pins. Pin change interrupts are sensed asynchronously and can wake the part from any sleep mode. INT0 can trigger on a low level, a rising edge or a falling edge; the edge modes need clkI/O, while the low level is sensed asynchronously and wakes from every sleep mode. A level interrupt fires for as long as the pin is low. Used to wake from Power-down, the level must last until the start-up time ends; if it goes away earlier the part wakes but takes no interrupt and continues after SLEEP.

Port A has eight bits and port B four. Every pin can be read, modified and written on its own with SBI/CBI, has a symmetrical driver that sinks and sources enough to drive LED displays, a selectable pull-up of supply-independent resistance and protection diodes to VCC and ground. Each port has three registers: PORTx (data), DDRx (direction) and PINx (input, read-only; writing one to a PINx bit toggles that PORTx bit). PUD in MCUCR turns every pull-up off. Enabling an alternate function on some pins leaves the rest of the port usable as I/O. Port pins go tri-state as soon as reset asserts, even with no clock; an input pulled low externally sources current when its pull-up is on.

DDxn = 1 makes the pin an output, driven to the PORTxn value; DDxn = 0 makes it an input, with the pull-up on when PORTxn = 1. Going from tri-state (00) to output high (11) passes through either pull-up on (01) or output low (10); the pull-up step is usually harmless, otherwise set PUD. Going from input with pull-up to output low likewise passes through tri-state or output high.

PINxn reads the pin whatever DDxn says, through a latch and flip-flop synchronizer that avoids metastability. An outside change reaches PINxn between half a clock and one and a half clocks later. Reading back a value software has just written needs a NOP between the OUT and the IN, for a one-clock delay.

In Power-down and Standby the input to each Schmitt trigger is clamped to ground, so floating or mid-supply inputs draw no current. Pins enabled as external interrupt inputs, and some alternate functions, override the clamp. A pin set for rising, falling or any-change external interrupt but not enabled, sitting high, sets its interrupt flag on waking, since the clamp itself makes the edge.

Give unused pins a defined level so floating inputs draw no current in reset, Active and Idle. The internal pull-up is simplest, though it is off during reset; where reset current matters use an external pull-up or pull-down. Do not tie unused pins straight to VCC or GND: a pin set as an output by mistake would then draw heavy current.

AREF on PA0 turns off the pin's pull-up and driver when REFS0 selects an external or capacitor-decoupled reference. AIN0 and AIN1 work best as inputs with the pull-up off. On PA5, DO overrides PORTA5 and drives the pin when DDA5 is set, while PORTA5 still controls the pull-up; MISO is forced to input in SPI master mode and follows DDA5 in slave mode. On PA6, the three-wire DI needs the pin set as input; MOSI is forced to input in slave mode and follows DDA6 in master mode. When the SPI forces a pin to input its pull-up is still under the PORTA bit. OC1A, OC1B and OC0B need their pin set as output and also carry the PWM output.

XTAL1 (PB0) serves every clock source except the internal RC oscillator, and XTAL2 (PB1) every source except the RC oscillator and an external clock; while serving as a clock pin neither can be I/O. CKOUT on PB2 outputs the system clock whenever its fuse is programmed, whatever PORTB2 and DDB2 hold. RESET on PB3 is on while RSTDISBL is unprogrammed, with the pull-up on and the driver and digital input off. With DWEN programmed and the lock bits unprogrammed, debugWIRE makes PB3 an open-drain bidirectional line with pull-up that carries the link to the debugger.

An 8-bit counter with two output compare channels (OC0A, OC0B), double-buffered compare registers, clear-on-match, glitch-free phase-correct PWM, a variable PWM period and a frequency generator. It raises three interrupts: overflow (TOV0) and the two compare matches (OCF0A, OCF0B), flagged in TIFR0 and masked in TIMSK0. TCNT0, OCR0A and OCR0B are 8-bit registers.

The clock select bits CS0[2:0] in TCCR0B choose the timer clock clkT0: the I/O clock through the prescaler, or an external signal on T0. With CS0[2:0] = 0 the counter stops, but the CPU can still read and write TCNT0, and a CPU write wins over any count or clear in the same cycle. WGM01:WGM00 in TCCR0A and WGM02 in TCCR0B set the counting sequence; TOV0 is set as the mode dictates and can interrupt the CPU.

TCNT0 is compared with OCR0A and OCR0B continuously. A match sets OCF0A or OCF0B on the following timer clock; the flag clears itself when its interrupt runs, or when software writes a one to it. In the PWM modes OCR0x is double-buffered and updates at TOP or BOTTOM so pulses never come out odd-length; in Normal and CTC modes the CPU writes OCR0x directly. Writing a one to FOC0x in a non-PWM mode forces a match on the pin without setting the flag or clearing the timer. Any CPU write to TCNT0 blocks a match in the next timer clock, even when stopped, so writing TCNT0 equal to OCR0x loses that match; nor should TCNT0 be written to BOTTOM while counting down.

A non-zero COM0x[1:0] lets the waveform generator take over the OC0x pin, but the pin still drives only when its DDR bit is set as output; set up OC0x before enabling the output, most simply with FOC0x in Normal mode. The internal OC0x state resets to 0 and survives a change of waveform mode. COM0x[1:0] is not double-buffered: a change takes effect at the next compare match, or at once through FOC0x in non-PWM modes. COM0x[1:0] = 0 means no action on a match.

WGM0[2:0] = 0: the counter only counts up, rolls over from 0xFF to 0x00 and sets TOV0 in the cycle it reaches zero, acting as a ninth bit that is set but not cleared by hardware. A new count may be written at any time. Compare matches can time interrupts; generating waveforms this way costs too much CPU time.

WGM0[2:0] = 2: the counter clears when it equals OCR0A, so OCR0A sets the top and with it the resolution. OCF0A can interrupt each time TOP is reached. OCR0A is not double-buffered in CTC mode: writing a value below the present count makes the counter run on to 0xFF and wrap before the next match. With COM0A[1:0] = 1 the pin toggles on each match, reaching at most fclk_I/O/2 with OCR0A = 0. TOV0 sets when the count passes MAX to 0x00.

WGM0[2:0] = 3 (TOP = 0xFF) or 7 (TOP = OCR0A): single-slope, counting BOTTOM to TOP and starting again, so the frequency can be twice that of phase-correct PWM. COM0x[1:0] = 2 gives non-inverted PWM (clear on match, set at BOTTOM); 3 gives inverted. With WGM02 set, COM0A[1:0] = 1 toggles OC0A on each match; OC0B has no toggle option. TOV0 sets at TOP. OCR0A at BOTTOM gives a narrow spike every MAX+1 timer clocks; at MAX the output stays high or low. Toggling on match gives a 50% square wave of up to fclk_I/O/2 with the double buffer active.

WGM0[2:0] = 1 (TOP = 0xFF) or 5 (TOP = OCR0A): dual-slope, counting up to TOP and back down, holding TOP for one timer clock. Non-inverted output (COM0x[1:0] = 2) clears on the up-count match and sets on the down-count match; 3 inverts it. With WGM02 set, COM0A0 = 1 toggles OC0A on matches; not for OC0B. TOV0 sets at BOTTOM. The symmetric output suits motor control. OCR0A at BOTTOM holds the non-inverted output low, at MAX high. To stay symmetric about BOTTOM the output can change without a match: when OCR0A leaves MAX, or when the count starts above OCR0A and so misses the up-count match.

The counter is synchronous; clkT0 acts as a clock enable on the I/O clock. TOV0 sets as the count moves from MAX to BOTTOM. OCF0B, and OCF0A outside the modes where OCR0A is TOP, set on the timer clock after TCNT0 equals OCR0x. In CTC and fast PWM with OCR0A as TOP, OCF0A sets and TCNT0 clears to BOTTOM on the timer clock after TOP.

A true 16-bit counter (16-bit PWM) with two output compare channels (OC1A, OC1B), double-buffered compare registers, an input capture unit with noise canceler, clear-on-match, glitch-free phase-correct PWM, a variable PWM period, a frequency generator and an external event counter. Four interrupts: TOV1, OCF1A, OCF1B and ICF1. TCNT1, OCR1A/B and ICR1 are 16-bit; TCCR1A/B are 8-bit with no access restriction. TOP can be a fixed value, OCR1A or ICR1: with OCR1A as TOP in a PWM mode, OC1A cannot output PWM but TOP is double-buffered; ICR1 as TOP frees OCR1A for PWM.

Register addresses, bit positions and interrupt vectors match the earlier AVR 16-bit timer. PWM10, PWM11 and CTC1 are renamed WGM10, WGM11 and WGM12 with unchanged function; FOC1A and FOC1B are added to TCCR1A and WGM13 to TCCR1B. A few special cases are not backward compatible.

CS1[2:0] in TCCR1B select clkT1 from the prescaler or the T1 pin; CS1[2:0] = 0 stops it. TCNT1 is two I/O locations: reading TCNT1L latches TCNT1H into the shared TEMP register, and writing TCNT1L copies TEMP into TCNT1H, so the full 16 bits move in one clock. Writing TCNT1 while counting can give unpredictable results in some modes. WGM1[3:0] in TCCR1A and TCCR1B set the counting sequence and when TOV1 sets.

An edge on ICP1, or on the analog comparator output when ACIC in ACSR is set, copies TCNT1 into ICR1 and sets ICF1 in the same system clock; ICF1 interrupts when ICIE1 = 1 and clears when serviced or written with a one. Read ICR1L before ICR1H. ICR1 can be written only in modes that use it as TOP, after WGM1[3:0] is set, high byte first. Changing the trigger source can itself trigger a capture, so clear ICF1 afterwards. ICP1 and the comparator output are sampled like the T1 pin. The capture input is live except in modes using ICR1 as TOP, and software can trigger a capture by driving the ICP1 port bit.

Setting ICNC1 in TCCR1B passes the capture signal through a four-sample filter: the edge detector sees a change only after four equal samples in a row. This adds four system clocks of delay before ICR1 updates. It runs on the system clock and ignores the prescaler.

If ICR1 is not read before the next event it is overwritten, so read it early in the interrupt handler; worst-case response depends on the longest other interrupt. Changing TOP while capturing is not recommended. To measure duty cycle, flip the edge select right after reading ICR1 and then clear ICF1 by writing a one; for frequency alone with an interrupt handler, clearing ICF1 is not needed. In Normal mode the interval between events must fit in the counter range, or the overflow interrupt or prescaler must stretch it.

TCNT1 is compared with OCR1A and OCR1B; a match sets OCF1x on the following timer clock and interrupts when OCIE1x = 1. Channel A can also define TOP and so the waveform period. OCR1x is double-buffered in all twelve PWM modes and written directly in Normal and CTC modes. OCR1x is changed only by writes, so reads do not use TEMP, but writes do: write OCR1xH first, then OCR1xL, which copies both bytes in one clock. FOC1x forces a match in non-PWM modes without setting the flag or clearing the timer. A TCNT1 write blocks a match in the next timer clock; writing TCNT1 equal to TOP in a variable-TOP PWM mode makes the counter skip TOP and run to 0xFFFF.

A non-zero COM1x[1:0] gives the OC1x pin to the waveform generator, with the DDR bit still setting the direction; the override is largely independent of the waveform mode. The internal OC1x state resets to 0 and is kept across mode changes; set it before enabling the pin, most simply with FOC1x in Normal mode. COM1x[1:0] is not double-buffered and acts from the next compare match, or at once through FOC1x in non-PWM modes. COM1x[1:0] has no effect on input capture.

WGM1[3:0] = 0: count up only, roll over from 0xFFFF to 0x0000, and set TOV1 as the count reaches zero, acting as a 17th bit that hardware sets but does not clear. The count can be rewritten at any time.

WGM1[3:0] = 4 (TOP = OCR1A) or 12 (TOP = ICR1): the counter clears on matching TOP; OCF1A or ICF1 flags it. Neither register is double-buffered in this mode, so a new TOP below the present count makes the counter run to 0xFFFF and wrap first; fast PWM with OCR1A as TOP (WGM1[3:0] = 15) avoids that. With COM1A[1:0] = 1, OC1A toggles on each match, up to fclk_I/O/2 when OCR1A = 0. TOV1 sets when the count passes MAX to 0x0000.

WGM1[3:0] = 5, 6 or 7 (TOP fixed at 0x00FF, 0x01FF or 0x03FF: 8, 9 or 10 bits), 14 (TOP = ICR1) or 15 (TOP = OCR1A). Single-slope, at up to twice the dual-slope frequency. Resolution runs from 2 bits (TOP = 0x0003) to 16 bits (TOP = MAX). TOV1 sets at TOP, and OCF1A or ICF1 in the same clock when that register is TOP. A new TOP must not be below any compare value or that channel never matches; with a fixed TOP the unused high bits of OCR1x are masked to zero when it is written. ICR1 is not double-buffered, so lowering it below the count makes the counter wrap through 0xFFFF; OCR1A as TOP is buffered and updates at TOP, so it suits a changing period while ICR1 suits a fixed one. COM1x[1:0] = 2 is non-inverted, 3 inverted. OCR1x = BOTTOM gives a narrow spike each TOP+1 timer clocks; OCR1x = TOP holds the output. COM1A[1:0] = 1 toggles OC1A for a 50% wave up to fclk_I/O/2 with OCR1A = 0.

WGM1[3:0] = 1, 2 or 3 (TOP fixed at 0x00FF, 0x01FF or 0x03FF), 10 (TOP = ICR1) or 11 (TOP = OCR1A). Dual-slope with TOP held one clock; resolution 2 to 16 bits. Non-inverted output clears on the up-count match and sets on the down-count match. TOV1 sets at BOTTOM; OCF1A or ICF1 sets at TOP, where OCR1x also takes its buffered value. Because OCR1x updates at TOP, changing TOP while running makes the two slopes of a period unequal and the output unsymmetrical; phase and frequency correct mode is recommended for a changing TOP. OCR1x = BOTTOM holds the non-inverted output low, OCR1x = TOP holds it high.

operation.topic: Timer/Counter1 phase and frequency correct PWM mode
operation.text: WGM1[3:0] = 8 (TOP = ICR1) or 9 (TOP = OCR1A). Dual-slope like phase correct mode, with 2 to 16 bits of resolution, but OCR1x takes its buffered value at BOTTOM, together with TOV1, so both slopes of every period are equal and the output stays symmetrical even as TOP changes. OCF1A or ICF1 sets at TOP. A new TOP must not be below any compare value. OCR1A as TOP suits a changing period; ICR1 as TOP leaves OCR1A free for PWM on OC1A.

clkT1 acts as a clock enable on the I/O clock. OCF1x sets on the timer clock after TCNT1 equals OCR1x. In CTC and fast PWM the count goes TOP to BOTTOM; in the two dual-slope modes it turns at TOP. TOV1 (fast PWM) and ICF1 (when ICR1 is TOP) set as TOP is passed, and OCR1x takes its new value at TOP; in phase and frequency correct mode the same happens at BOTTOM.

TCNT1, OCR1A/B and ICR1 are read and written a byte at a time through one 8-bit TEMP register shared by all of Timer/Counter1's 16-bit registers. Write the high byte first, then the low byte, which moves both in one clock; read the low byte first, which latches the high byte into TEMP. Reading OCR1A/B does not use TEMP. C compilers handle the order. An interrupt that touches any 16-bit timer register between the two accesses corrupts TEMP, so main code that shares TEMP with an interrupt must disable interrupts around the access. When several registers share the same high byte it need be written only once.

Timer/Counter0 and Timer/Counter1 share one free-running prescaler but select from it independently. CSn[2:0] = 1 runs the timer at the full I/O clock; the taps give fclk_I/O/8, /64, /256 or /1024. Because the prescaler runs regardless of the clock select, the first count after enabling a prescaled clock (CSn[2:0] = 2 to 5) comes 1 to N+1 system clocks later, N being the divisor. Resetting the prescaler (PSR10) synchronises the timer to program flow.

A signal on T0 or T1 can clock its timer: CSn[2:0] = 7 counts rising edges, 6 falling edges. The pin is sampled every system clock and passed through an edge detector, which delays the count by 2.5 to 3.5 system clocks. Switch the input on or off only while Tn has been steady for a system clock, or a false count can occur. Each half-period must exceed one system clock: with 50% duty fExtClk < fclk_I/O/2, and less than fclk_I/O/2.5 is recommended to allow for oscillator tolerance. An external clock cannot be prescaled.

The Universal Serial Interface gives the hardware for two-wire (master or slave) and three-wire (master or slave) synchronous transfers, with a data-received interrupt, wake-up from Idle, and in two-wire mode a start condition detector that can interrupt and wake the part from every sleep mode including Power-down. Software supplies the protocol, with faster transfers and less code than a software-only link.

The 8-bit USIDR holds the data in and out; each transfer is also copied to the USI buffer register USIBR for later reading, while USIDR itself must be read quickly. USIDR's top bit drives the output pin through a transparent latch, so output changes on the clock edge opposite to input sampling; input is always sampled from DI. A readable, writable 4-bit counter is clocked with the data register and interrupts on overflow; with an external clock it counts both edges, so it counts edges rather than bits. The clock comes from the USCK pin, the Timer/Counter0 compare match, or software. In two-wire mode the clock control unit may interrupt on a start condition and hold SCL low after a start or a counter overflow.

Uses DI, DO and USCK and follows SPI modes 0 and 1, with no slave-select pin (software can provide it). After eight USCK clocks two connected USIDRs have swapped contents, and USIOIF marks the transfer done. The master makes the clock in software, toggling USCK through PORTA or by writing USITC in USICR. In external clock mode 0 (USICS0 = 0) DI is sampled on rising edges and DO shifts on falling edges; mode 1 uses the opposite edges. A transfer: load USIDR and enable the output through DDRA at least half a USCK cycle before the first sampling edge, reset the counter, then give eight clock pulses (16 edges) until the counter overflows; the overflow interrupt wakes the CPU from Idle.

operation.topic: USI as SPI master or slave
operation.text: As a master, a loop that writes USIWM0, USICS1, USICLK and USITC to USICR sixteen times shifts one byte, with DO and USCK set as outputs in DDRA; the byte to send goes in USIDR first and the received byte is read back from USIDR. Alternating two USICR words without a loop gives the fastest master clock, fSCK = fCK/2. As a slave, USIWM0 and USICS1 set once select three-wire mode with the external clock; each transfer writes USIDR, clears USIOIF and waits for it to set again.

Follows the TWI (I2C) protocol at the physical level on SDA and SCL, without output slew limiting or input filtering. The clock control unit serves the slave alone; the master makes the clock in software by toggling USCK through PORTA, and must check SCL has really been released after each rising edge because the slave may stretch it. Shifting on negative edges is the useful setting. The protocol, not the hardware, sets the data direction.

The master signals a start by pulling SDA low with SCL high, by writing a zero to USIDR bit 7 or clearing the PORTA bit, with the DDR bit set. The slave's start detector sets USISIF, can interrupt, and holds SCL low after the master's falling edge on SCL until software clears the flag and resets the counter. The slave shifts in data on rising SCL edges; after the address and R/W bit the counter overflows and SCL is held low. An unaddressed slave releases SCL and waits for the next start. An addressed slave sets the counter to 14 before releasing SCL so it can pull SDA low through the acknowledge, then may hold SCL again. Bytes follow in one direction until a stop or repeated start. A slave that cannot take more data leaves the last byte unacknowledged; to end a read, the master drives the acknowledge bit low once the final byte is in.

Active only in two-wire mode. SDA is delayed by 40 to 100 ns so SCL is sampled cleanly. The detector is asynchronous and can wake the part from Power-down, but the oscillator start-up time set by the CKSEL fuses then adds to the SCL hold time the protocol must tolerate.

SCL and SCK run at most at fCK/2, which is also the top data rate in two- and three-wire modes. In two-wire slave mode the clock control unit holds SCL low until the slave is ready, which can lower the actual rate.

In three-wire mode USIDR can carry a half-duplex asynchronous UART smaller and faster than a software one. The 4-bit counter alone is a counter with overflow interrupt (counting both edges when externally clocked); combined with an 8-bit timer it makes a 12-bit counter; preset to 0xF and clocked by the pin (selected with USICS1) it acts as an extra edge-triggered external interrupt; and strobing its clock gives a software interrupt.

Compares AIN0 (positive) with AIN1 (negative) and sets ACO when AIN0 is higher. It has its own interrupt, on a rising, falling or toggling output, and can trigger Timer/Counter1 input capture (ACIC). The internal bandgap can replace AIN0 (ACBG). ACO is synchronised, adding 1 to 2 clock cycles of delay. Using the ADC multiplexer needs PRADC in PRR cleared. Setting ACD switches the comparator off to save power in Active and Idle; clear ACIE before changing ACD or an interrupt may fire.

With ACME in ADCSRB set and the ADC switched off (ADEN = 0), the ADC multiplexer selects one of ADC0 to ADC7 as the comparator's negative input in place of AIN1. With ACME cleared or ADEN set, AIN1 is the negative input.

A 10-bit successive-approximation converter: INL of 1 LSB, ±2 LSB absolute accuracy, 13 µs per conversion, 15 kSPS at full resolution. A nine-channel multiplexer gives eight single-ended inputs referred to GND, twelve differential pairs through a gain stage of 1x (0 dB) or 20x (26 dB), and the internal temperature sensor. Input range is 0 to VCC; references are VCC (single-ended channels), the internal 1.1 V reference, or an external voltage on AREF with the internal reference off. A sample-and-hold keeps the input steady during conversion. Also: left-adjusted result, free-running or single conversion, auto-triggering from interrupt sources, a conversion-complete interrupt, a sleep-mode noise canceler, unipolar or bipolar input, and input polarity reversal.

Clear PRADC in PRR and set ADEN in ADCSRA; the reference and channel selections take effect only once ADEN is set. With ADEN clear the ADC draws no power, so switch it off before power-saving sleep. REFS[1:0] in ADMUX selects the reference, MUX bits the channel and gain (MUX0 sets the gain). Any input can be single-ended; adjacent inputs pair as differential channels, and any input can also pair with ADC3. Single-ended channels bypass the gain amplifier. Selecting ADC0, ADC3 or ADC7 as both inputs measures the gain stage offset, which can then be subtracted from later conversions at the same gain, leaving under 1 LSB of offset.

The 10-bit result sits in ADCH and ADCL, right-adjusted unless ADLAR in ADCSRB is set. With a left-adjusted result and 8 bits enough, read only ADCH; otherwise read ADCL first, then ADCH. Reading ADCL locks both registers until ADCH is read, so a conversion finishing in between is lost, though its interrupt still fires.

Writing a one to ADSC starts a single conversion; ADSC reads one until it finishes, however the conversion began. A channel change during a conversion waits for it to finish. Setting ADATE enables auto-triggering from the source chosen by ADTS in ADCSRB: a rising edge on the trigger resets the ADC prescaler and starts a conversion, giving fixed intervals; edges during a conversion, or a trigger still high at its end, start nothing. The trigger's interrupt flag sets even with its interrupt disabled, and must be cleared before the next event can trigger. Using ADIF as the trigger gives Free Running mode: each conversion starts as the last ends, whether or not ADIF is cleared, after a first conversion started by ADSC.

For full 10-bit resolution the ADC clock must be 50 kHz to 200 kHz; for less resolution it may be higher, but not above 1 MHz is recommended. A 7-bit prescaler set by ADPS in ADCSRA divides the CPU clock by 2 to 128, suiting any CPU clock above 100 kHz; it runs while ADEN is set and is held reset otherwise. A single conversion starts on the next rising ADC clock edge after ADSC is set. A normal conversion takes 13 ADC clocks with sample-and-hold 1.5 clocks in; the first after ADEN is set takes 25 clocks, sampling at 13.5, to initialise the analog circuits. On completion the result is written, ADIF sets and in single mode ADSC clears. An auto-triggered conversion samples two ADC clocks after the trigger edge, plus three CPU clocks of synchronisation; in Free Running mode the next conversion starts at once with ADSC kept high.

MUX and REFS in ADMUX pass through a temporary register: the selection follows writes until a conversion starts, then is frozen for the sampling time, and resumes in the last ADC clock before the conversion ends. Since a conversion starts on the ADC clock edge after ADSC is written, wait one ADC clock after ADSC before writing new values. With ADATE and ADEN both set a trigger can come at any time; ADMUX is safe to change when ADATE or ADEN is clear, at least one ADC clock after a trigger during a conversion, or after a conversion but before the triggering flag is cleared, and then applies to the next conversion. In single mode select the channel before starting; in Free Running mode select it before the first conversion, and note that after a change the next result still comes from the old channel.

VREF sets the conversion range; single-ended inputs above it read close to 0x3FF. It can be VCC, the internal 1.1 V reference (from the bandgap VBG through an amplifier), or AREF. Discard the first result after switching reference, which may be inaccurate.

Conversions can run during sleep to cut noise from the CPU and I/O. With the ADC enabled, idle, in single conversion mode and its interrupt enabled, entering ADC Noise Reduction or Idle mode starts a conversion once the CPU halts; the ADC interrupt then wakes the CPU. If another interrupt wakes it first, that one runs and the ADC interrupt follows on completion, with the CPU staying awake until the next sleep instruction. Other sleep modes do not switch the ADC off; clear ADEN before them to avoid excess current.

Each ADCn pin carries its pin capacitance and leakage whether or not it is selected. When selected, the source charges a sample-and-hold capacitance of 14 pF (worst case, including stray capacitance) through a series resistance of 1 to 100 kΩ, referred to VCC/2. Sources of about 10 kΩ or less make the sampling time negligible; higher impedances need longer, and slowly varying signals are best fed from low impedance. Frequency content above the Nyquist frequency (fADC/2) should be removed with a low-pass filter before the input.

Keep analog paths short and over the analog ground plane, away from fast digital tracks; do not switch port pins used as digital outputs during a conversion; place bypass capacitors as close to the VCC and GND pins as possible. ADC Noise Reduction mode is recommended where accuracy matters, especially above a 1 MHz system clock or when reading the temperature sensor; good external bypassing lessens the need for it.

An n-bit single-ended ADC spans GND to VREF in 2^n steps, codes 0 to 2^n-1. Offset: the first transition (0x000 to 0x001) against its ideal at 0.5 LSB; ideal 0 LSB. Gain error: after offset correction, the last transition (0x3FE to 0x3FF) against its ideal 1.5 LSB below full scale; ideal 0 LSB. INL: after offset and gain correction, the largest departure of any transition from ideal; ideal 0 LSB. DNL: the largest departure of a code width from 1 LSB; ideal 0 LSB. Quantisation error: always ±0.5 LSB. Absolute accuracy: the largest departure of any uncorrected transition from ideal, combining all of these; ideal ±0.5 LSB.
The ADC starts in unipolar mode; writing BIN in ADCSRB to one selects bipolar mode, in which the negative input may be higher than the positive one.

The on-chip temperature sensor is single-ended channel ADC8, enabled by writing 100010 to MUX[5:0] in ADMUX, with the internal 1.1 V reference selected, read in single conversion mode. Its output is linear in temperature at about 1 LSB per °C. A single calibration at room temperature typically gives ±10 °C; calibrating at two temperatures does better. The output varies from chip to chip, so software calibration with a slope k (typically very close to 1.0, and may be left out for a one-point calibration) and an offset TOS is used.

A one-wire, bidirectional on-chip debug link that controls program flow, executes AVR instructions in the CPU and programs the non-volatile memories. It emulates every on-chip function, digital and analog, except the RESET pin, runs in real time and non-intrusively with the electrical behaviour of the real part, and supports C and assembler symbolic debugging and unlimited software breakpoints. With the DWEN fuse programmed and the lock bits unprogrammed, the RESET pin becomes an open-drain bidirectional line with pull-up that carries the link. The system clock stays the one the CKSEL fuses choose.

A breakpoint replaces an instruction in Flash with BREAK and stores the original, which runs when execution continues; BREAK can also be placed in the program by hand. Each breakpoint change reprograms the Flash, which uses up Flash data retention, so parts used for debugging should not be shipped.

With debugWIRE on, external reset is not supported since dW shares the RESET pin. I/O is emulated exactly at full speed, but some I/O registers need care when accessed with the CPU stopped. The link is asynchronous and locks to the system clock, so changing the clock in software (for example CLKPS) can break it, and clocks below 100 kHz may cause trouble. A programmed DWEN keeps parts of the clock system running in every sleep mode, raising sleep current; leave DWEN unprogrammed when not debugging. The DWDR register passes data from the running program to the debugger and is not a general-purpose register.

The part can load and store its own program code over any interface. The SPM instruction is off until the SELFPRGEN fuse is programmed (0). Flash is written a page at a time from a temporary page buffer filled one word at a time by SPM, either before a page erase or between erase and write. To change part of a page, keep the rest (for example in the buffer) before erasing and write it back; filling before the erase allows read-modify-write, filling after it does not. The buffer can be filled in any order. Page erase and page write must address the same page.

operation.topic: SPM page erase, buffer load and page write
operation.text: Page erase: put a page address in PCPAGE of Z, load SPMCSR with 00000011 and run SPM no more than four cycles later; R1:R0 are ignored and the CPU halts during the erase. Buffer load: word address in Z (PCWORD), data in R1:R0, SPMCSR loaded with 00000001, then SPM no more than four cycles later. The buffer clears after a page write, on writing CTPB in SPMCSR, and after a system reset; each address can be written once per buffer fill. An EEPROM write during page loading loses all loaded data. Page write: page address in PCPAGE with the other Z bits zero, SPMCSR loaded with 00000101, then SPM no more than four cycles later; the CPU halts during the write.

The Z-pointer (R31:R30) addresses SPM. The low bits of the program counter select the word within a page (PCWORD) and the high bits select which page (PCPAGE). LPM addresses Flash by byte and so also uses Z0.
An EEPROM write blocks all software programming of Flash, and reading fuses and lock bits from software, while it lasts; check that EEPE in EECR is clear before writing SPMCSR.

operation.topic: Reading lock, fuse and signature bytes from software
operation.text: Firmware can read the fuse and lock bits and the device signature imprint table; programmed bits read as 0, unprogrammed as 1. Load Z, set RFLB and SPMEN in SPMCSR (RSIG and SPMEN for the signature table), and issue LPM within three CPU cycles; the byte arrives in the LPM destination register. RFLB and SPMEN clear when the read completes, or if no LPM follows within three cycles or no SPM within four. Z = 0x0001 returns the lock bits (LB2 in bit 1, LB1 in bit 0), 0x0000 the fuse low byte, 0x0003 the fuse high byte, 0x0002 the fuse extended byte; for the signature table Z holds the table index.

Too low a VCC can corrupt Flash in two ways: a Flash write needs a minimum voltage, and the CPU can misexecute instructions. Either measure suffices: hold RESET active while the supply is too low, using the brown-out detector if its level matches the operating voltage or an external low-VCC reset otherwise (a write in progress completes if the voltage allows); or keep the core in Power-down sleep during low VCC so SPMCSR cannot be written by stray code.

Two lock bits, LB1 and LB2, are unprogrammed (1) by default and can be programmed (0) for two further protection modes; only a chip erase returns them to 1. There is no separate boot loader section: with SELFPRGEN programmed SPM works over the whole Flash. A programmed DWEN lets debugWIRE read the program memory even with lock bits set, so DWEN must be unprogrammed where lock-bit security is needed.

Three fuse bytes: extended, high and low. A programmed fuse reads 0. LB1 programmed locks the fuses, so program fuses before lock bits; chip erase leaves the fuses unchanged. Fuse values are latched on entering programming mode and take effect on leaving it, except EESAVE, which acts as soon as it is programmed; they are also latched at power-up. After RSTDISBL is programmed only high-voltage serial programming can change fuses or program the part. SPIEN cannot be reached from SPI programming. Programming WDTON disables the watchdog interrupt.

A separate memory area holding the three signature bytes and the oscillator calibration byte; most of it is reserved. The signature identifies the device and can be read in serial and high-voltage programming, even when the part is locked, and by firmware. During reset the calibration byte is copied into OSCCAL automatically so the RC oscillator runs at its calibrated frequency.

Flash and EEPROM can be programmed over SPI (SCK, MOSI in, MISO out) with RESET held at GND; the Programming Enable instruction must come first. Running from the internal oscillator, CLKI needs no clock. In serial mode an EEPROM write erases the byte itself, so no chip erase is needed first. Chip erase sets every Flash and EEPROM location to 0xFF. A valid clock per the CKSEL fuses must be present. SCK low and high periods must each exceed 2 CPU clocks below 12 MHz and 3 CPU clocks at 12 MHz and above. Data in is clocked on the rising SCK edge, data out on the falling edge.

Power up with RESET and SCK at 0; if the programmer cannot hold SCK low at power-up, pulse RESET high after SCK is 0, for at least tRST plus two CPU clocks. Wait at least 20 ms, then send Programming Enable on MOSI. In sync, the second byte (0x53) echoes back while the third is sent; send all four bytes regardless, and if 0x53 did not echo, pulse RESET and try again. Flash is written a page at a time: load each byte with Load Program Memory Page and the 5 LSBs of the address, low byte before high byte, then store that page with Write Program Memory Page and the 3 MSBs. EEPROM can be written a byte at a time (each byte is erased automatically first) or a page at a time (2 address LSBs per load, 4 MSBs on write; only loaded bytes change). Without RDY/BSY polling, wait tWD_FLASH or tWD_EEPROM before the next page or byte; accessing the interface before a Flash write finishes can corrupt it. 0xFF need not be written to a chip-erased part. Read instructions verify any location on MISO. Finish by setting RESET high; to power off, set RESET to 1 and remove VCC.

Programs and verifies Flash, EEPROM, lock bits and fuses with 11.5 V to 12.5 V on RESET and VCC at 4.5 V to 5.5 V. Data enters on SDI (PA6), instructions on SII (PA5) and data leaves on SDO (PA4), all clocked by SCI (PB0), whose period must be at least 220 ns; PA0 to PA2 are the Prog_enable pins, held at 0 to enter the mode. Data is clocked on the rising SCI edge.

Set the Prog_enable pins to 000 and RESET and VCC to 0 V. Apply 4.5 V to 5.5 V to VCC so that it reaches at least 1.8 V within 20 µs; after 20 µs to 60 µs apply 11.5 V to 12.5 V to RESET. Keep Prog_enable unchanged 10 µs or longer once RESET is high so the entry code latches, release Prog_enable[2] after tHVRST, and wait at least 300 µs before sending instructions on SDI/SII. If VCC cannot rise that fast: apply VCC, watch it, and apply the high voltage to RESET as VCC passes 0.9 V to 1.1 V; hold Prog_enable 10 µs, release Prog_enable[2] to avoid contention with SDO on that pin, and wait for VCC to reach 4.5 V to 5.5 V before instructions. Leave the mode by powering down or taking RESET to 0 V.

The loaded command and address are kept, so a command is loaded once for many locations, the address high byte only for a new 256-word Flash or 256-byte EEPROM window (also for signature reads), and 0xFF need not be written after a chip erase (EEPROM included unless EESAVE is programmed). Chip erase clears Flash, EEPROM (kept if EESAVE is programmed) and the lock bits, the lock bits only after Flash is fully erased, and leaves the fuses; it must precede reprogramming Flash or EEPROM. After a chip erase, page program or fuse/lock write, wait until SDO goes high. Flash and EEPROM are each written by loading the write command, filling its page buffer, programming it, repeating per page, and ending with No Operation; in high-voltage mode EEPROM bytes are not erased automatically. Reads load the read command, then return each byte on SDO. Power off by setting SCI to 0 and RESET to 1, then removing VCC.
The highest clock the part runs at is set by VCC: 4 MHz at 1.8 V rising in a straight line to 20 MHz at 4.5 V, and 20 MHz from 4.5 V to 5.5 V.

Factory calibration sets the internal oscillator to 8.0 MHz within ±10 % at 3 V and 25 °C. Calibrating it in the application at a fixed voltage (1.8 V to 5.5 V) and fixed temperature (-40 °C to +85 °C) can bring it to ±1 % anywhere from 7.3 MHz to 8.1 MHz. Its frequency moves with voltage and temperature.

In serial programming MOSI is set up before the rising edge of SCK (tOVSH) and held after it (tSHOX); SCK high and low times are tSHSL and tSLSH, and MISO changes after the falling edge. Data goes most significant bit first, and each bit is sampled on the rising edge of SCK.
In high-voltage serial programming SDI (PA6) and SII (PA5) are set up before the rising edge of SCI (PB0) (tIVSH) and held after it (tSHIX); SDO (PA4) is valid tSHOV after the rising edge of SCI.

The typical characteristic curves show typical behaviour only. They rest largely on simulation and on characterisation of similar devices built on the same process, and none of them is tested in production. During characterisation devices ran faster than the test limits; that is no guarantee of operation above the speed the ordering code gives. Current was measured with every I/O pin an input with its pull-up on, clocked from a rail-to-rail sine generator. Power-down current does not depend on the clock source. The watchdog's own current is the power-down current with it on less the power-down current with it off. The main influences on supply current are VCC and clock frequency; I/O loading, I/O switching rate, the code that runs and ambient temperature also count.

Each module switched on in the power reduction register PRR adds current in active and idle mode. The added current is given as typical absolute figures at three supply and clock points, and as a share of the active or idle current with an external clock, which holds at other voltages and frequencies.
